problem: Existing object-goal navigation methods rely on single visual observations or simple semantic matching, so they do not capture 3D relationships between objects, which leads to inefficient path planning. The gap between visual and language features also hurts target identification.
motivation: Object-goal navigation in complex indoor scenes needs spatial understanding of how objects relate in 3D and reliable recognition of the target. The paper argues that explicit 3D relational modeling combined with aligned visual-language features should improve spatial cognition and navigation efficiency.
key_idea: Build a latent 3D scene graph from depth perception to model inter-object 3D relations, and use multimodal pretraining to align visual and language features, all in an end-to-end navigator (LSGAP).
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations or analysis can be cited. The abstract claims that explicit 3D relation modeling and visual-language alignment are complementary for target recognition and path planning.
method: Latent 3D scene graph: constructs a latent graph of object nodes and their 3D relationships using depth perception (details not available from abstract)
Depth perception: uses depth to lift observations into 3D spatial relations between objects
Aligned visual-language perception: multimodal pretraining to align visual and language features for target recognition
End-to-end navigator: jointly trained architecture making navigation decisions from the scene graph and aligned features
